episode_title: The Fourth Master: Kondo Isami and the Death He Was Refused
youtube_title: The Farm Boy Who Led Japan's Deadliest Swordsmen and Died Like a Criminal
youtube_description:
He was born a farmer's third son with no legal right to carry a sword, and he ended up commanding the most feared armed force in Japan. In the summer of 1867 the shogunate formally made him a samurai. Four months later the government that granted it collapsed, and the men who won refused him a samurai's death and beheaded him in a public execution ground. This is the story of Kondo Isami.

scenes.narration: Kondo Isami was born in the autumn of 1834 in Kami-ishihara, a farming village on the Musashi plain west of Edo. His name then was Miyagawa Katsugoro, third son of a reasonably prosperous farmer. The Tama district he grew up in was shogunal land, held and taxed directly by the Tokugawa, and unusually proud of the fact. Its farmers were not samurai and by law never could be, yet many of them practised swordsmanship in barns and shrine courtyards, and thought of themselves as the shogun's own men. That distinction would eventually kill him.

scenes.narration: At fifteen he was taken into a small Edo training hall called the Shieikan, which taught a country style named Tennen Rishin-ryu — crude by the standards of the great urban schools, fought with oversized wooden swords, built entirely around surviving a real fight in a confined space. The master, Kondo Shusuke, had no heir. Within a few years he adopted the farm boy outright, and Miyagawa Katsugoro became Kondo Isami. He had been given a name, a lineage and a household. None of it made him a samurai. In law he was still a peasant holding a sword.

scenes.narration: In 1861 he was formally installed as the fourth master of the school, at a public demonstration in the grounds of a shrine at Fuchu. He was twenty-six. The men who trained with him then were mostly farm boys and village toughs, with a few exceptions: a minor retainer's son named Okita Soji, barely out of his teens and already the most dangerous swordsman in the room, and a medicine peddler from a nearby village, cold and exacting, called Hijikata Toshizo. They had a school, a lineage and no war to use either in. Then the shogunate began recruiting.

scenes.narration: In the spring of 1863 the government began enlisting swordsmen of any birth to escort the fourteenth shogun to Kyoto, where imperial loyalists were killing officials in the street. Kondo took his students and signed up. They marched west with more than two hundred men, and the scheme fell apart on arrival: the organiser turned out to be an imperial loyalist himself and ordered everyone back to Edo. Thirteen men refused. Kondo was one of them. He stayed in Kyoto with no orders, no money and no authority whatsoever, and went looking for a patron.

scenes.narration: The Aizu domain took them on as auxiliaries, and by that autumn they had a name: Shinsengumi, the Newly Selected Corps. Command was shared with a violent Mito masterless samurai named Serizawa Kamo, who extorted merchants and burned down a shop over a refused loan. In the autumn of 1863 men entered his lodging at night and killed him in his sleep, and they were almost certainly Kondo's own. From that night there was one commander. Kondo led from the front and left the enforcing of discipline to the vice-commander who had trained beside him at the Edo hall.

scenes.narration: The corps regulations were short and absolute. Do not deviate from the way of the warrior. Do not leave the corps. Do not fight private duels. The penalty attached to each was the same — seppuku. Over four years more Shinsengumi died under their own rules than at the hands of any enemy, and every one of those orders carried Kondo's authority. In 1865 the corps' general manager, a founding member from the Edo training hall, tried to walk away. He was hunted down, brought back, and made to cut himself open. Kondo approved it and said nothing.

scenes.narration: On the humid night of the eighth of July, 1864, the corps surrounded an inn called the Ikedaya, where loyalist radicals were finalising a plan to burn Kyoto in a high wind and carry the emperor off in the confusion. Kondo went up the stairs with three men. He fought in the dark of a low wooden building for nearly two hours before the larger detachment arrived and sealed the exits. By morning the plot was finished and the Shinsengumi were the most feared armed force in Japan. He wrote home about it, and the pride is impossible to miss.

scenes.narration: He was proud of the sword he had carried that night, a blade bearing the signature of the great smith Nagasone Kotetsu, and he told his family it had come through the fighting without a single chip. Money and status followed the victory, and something in him shifted. He took better quarters, kept mistresses, travelled by palanquin, and began behaving less like the head of a country fencing school than a lord with retainers. In 1864 several of his own founding officers put their names to a written complaint about it. He absorbed the reprimand and changed almost nothing.

scenes.narration: In the summer of 1867 the thing he had wanted his whole life arrived. The Shinsengumi were made direct retainers of the shogun, and Kondo Isami, a farmer's third son from Kami-ishihara, was formally a samurai in Tokugawa service. It lasted four months. In November the fifteenth shogun handed his authority back to the emperor. Weeks later, riding home from a meeting in Fushimi, Kondo was ambushed by men avenging an officer he had purged from the corps. A pistol ball shattered his right shoulder. The fourth master of Tennen Rishin-ryu would never use a sword properly again.

scenes.narration: At the end of January 1868 the two sides finally met south of Kyoto, at Toba and Fushimi. The shogunate had roughly three times the men and lost in four days. The imperial army had modern rifles and field artillery; the Shinsengumi went in with swords and were broken as a fighting unit. Kondo was not among them. His right arm was useless, and he watched the corps he had spent five years building come apart from a distance, then boarded a steamship for Edo with the wounded. He arrived in a city whose government had stopped functioning.

scenes.narration: In March 1868 he was given one last command: a newly raised force sent west to hold Kofu castle before the imperial army could reach it. He took the alias Okubo Yamato and the bearing of the lord he had nearly become, and the road ran straight through the Tama villages where he had grown up. They came out to watch the farm boy pass as a shogunal commander. The delay cost him the castle. Government troops occupied Kofu first, and at Katsunuma his half-trained men met artillery in the rain and broke inside two hours.

scenes.narration: He fell back through Edo and regrouped at Nagareyama, north-east of the city, with roughly two hundred men still under arms. In late April 1868 imperial troops surrounded the camp at dawn. Kondo walked out alone to negotiate, still calling himself Okubo Yamato, offering himself in exchange for letting his men disperse. It very nearly worked. Then a former Shinsengumi officer he had once driven out of the corps was brought forward to look at the prisoner's face, and named him. The most wanted man in Japan had just handed himself over.

scenes.narration: He was taken to Itabashi, on the northern road out of Edo, and spent three weeks arguing about who he was. He had been a retainer of the shogun, and a samurai was entitled to die by his own hand. But the officers holding him were largely from Tosa, and Tosa believed the Shinsengumi had murdered Sakamoto Ryoma the previous winter, a killing most historians now attribute to another unit entirely. They refused him the blade. On the seventeenth of May, 1868, Kondo Isami was beheaded in a public execution ground as a common criminal. He was thirty-three.

scenes.narration: His head was carried to Kyoto and set up beside the Sanjo riverbank, the same stretch of gravel where the corps had once displayed the heads of men it hunted. It vanished afterwards and has never been accounted for. Before the end he wrote a poem in Chinese comparing himself to the defenders of a Tang city who held out long after any hope of relief was gone. Three temples now claim to hold some part of his remains and none of them can prove it. What his family kept, and still keeps, are his letters.

scenes.narration: There is a coda to the sword. Specialists who have examined the blade tradition around Kondo's celebrated Kotetsu generally conclude that it was not one — that the farmer's son so proud of carrying a masterpiece by one of Japan's greatest smiths had been sold, or given, a very good forgery. He appears to have died believing in it. It is hard to think of a more exact image of the man: a borrowed signature on a borrowed identity, held onto with more conviction than most of the people born to the real thing ever managed.

scenes.narration: For a century the Shinsengumi were remembered as hired blades on the wrong side of history, and Kondo as the least interesting of them, a figurehead standing in front of his vice-commander's ruthlessness. Fiction eventually rescued the corps, but it rescued Hijikata first, and Kondo has stayed in that shadow ever since. His own district never accepted the verdict. The Tama villages still gather at his grave every spring, and the school he inherited from a childless Edo swordmaster is still taught out there, unbroken, by the descendants of farmers.

scenes.narration: Two men from the same country training hall, on the same losing side, ended differently. Hijikata died in a Western uniform on a northern battlefield, commanding an army, with a rifle line behind him. Kondo died kneeling on flat ground outside Edo, unarmed, in front of men who would not concede he had ever been a samurai. He had spent his whole life assembling that claim out of nothing — a name, a school, a code, a corps, a stipend — and at the end the only piece of it that could not be taken back was the code.

scenes.narration: Next time on Samurai Chronicles. A general sent west by his own government to crush an emperor's rebellion, who changed sides on the road, destroyed the regime he served, and personally put that emperor back on the throne. Three years later he drove the same emperor out of Kyoto, installed a rival in his place, and took the title of shogun for himself. Japan called him a traitor for the next six hundred years. The government he built lasted more than two centuries. Ashikaga Takauji.
